questions.question: How do Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow differ as embedded servers in Spring Boot, and how do you switch between them?
questions.title: Embedded Server Configuration (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow)
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot defaults to **embedded Tomcat** but supports Jetty and Undertow by excluding `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` and adding the desired alternative — a single dependency swap, no code changes. **Tomcat is the most battle-tested**; **Undertow offers the lowest memory footprint and highest servlet throughput**; **Jetty is a solid middle ground** with strong WebSocket and SSE support. All three are configured through the `server.*` property namespace. For reactive WebFlux apps the default is **Netty** — an event-loop server that suits non-blocking I/O.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the trade-offs between the three servers and can justify a server choice for a given workload
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that switching embedded servers requires code changes — it is a single dependency swap because Spring Boot abstracts the server behind `WebServer`/`ServletWebServerFactory` interfaces
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that for reactive WebFlux applications Netty is the default (not Tomcat), and explain how to customise the server via `WebServerFactoryCustomizer` for connection pooling, thread counts, and SSL configuration

sections.title: Embedded Means Inside the JAR — and Switching Is a Dependency Change
sections.content:
Spring Boot bundles the web server **inside your application JAR**. Running `java -jar app.jar` starts the server from `main()` — no external Tomcat install, no WAR deployment, no app-server admin console. This is the model that makes Boot containerizable and self-contained.

The common misconception is that switching from Tomcat to Jetty or Undertow requires code changes.
- **It's a single dependency swap** in your build file — exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`.
- Spring Boot's `WebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration` detects which server is on the classpath and configures it automatically.

What's less obvious is **why you'd switch** and what each server is actually optimized for.
- Tomcat is the default because it's the most widely understood, has the largest ecosystem of documentation, and handles most workloads well.
- Jetty uses less memory under idle conditions and handles large numbers of long-lived connections (WebSocket, SSE) more efficiently.
- Undertow is the fastest on raw throughput benchmarks.
- For **reactive WebFlux applications, the default is Netty** — an event-loop server purpose-built for non-blocking I/O.

sections.content:
```mermaid

```

sections.title: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow vs Netty — When Each Server Wins
sections.content:
The choice depends on your workload pattern, not just benchmark numbers.

| Aspect | Tomcat | Jetty | Undertow | Netty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Default for** | Spring MVC (servlet) | Manual swap | Manual swap | Spring WebFlux (reactive) |
| **I/O model** | Thread-per-request | Thread-per-request + async | Non-blocking (XNIO) | Event loop |
| **Memory at idle** | Higher baseline | Lower idle footprint | Moderate | Lowest |
| **WebSocket / SSE** | Good | Better for many connections | Good | Best |
| **Raw throughput** | Good | Good | Highest for servlet | Highest for reactive |
| **Ecosystem** | Most docs, most community support | Strong Eclipse ecosystem | Red Hat backed | Widely used in reactive |
| **When to choose** | General purpose, no reason to switch | Many idle connections, memory-constrained | Maximum servlet throughput | Reactive / WebFlux apps |

**The practical recommendation:** stick with Tomcat unless you have a measured reason to switch. Most applications are not I/O-bound enough for the server choice to matter.

sections.title: Switching Servers — The Maven and Gradle Recipes
sections.content:
**Maven — switch to Undertow**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle — switch to Jetty**

```groovy
implementation('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web') {
    exclude group: 'org.springframework.boot', module: 'spring-boot-starter-tomcat'
}
implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jetty'
```

**Verification**
- Restart and check the startup log: `Tomcat started on port(s)`, `Jetty started`, or `Undertow started`
- `/actuator/info` and the startup banner show the active server
- All `server.*` properties continue to work — port, SSL, compression, error pages

**Common server.* properties (server-agnostic)**

```properties
server.port=8080
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.min-response-size=2KB
server.ssl.enabled=true
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-password=${KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
```

sections.title: Programmatic Customization with WebServerFactoryCustomizer
Embedded Server Choice Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When Tomcat helps:**
- Default Spring MVC applications with no measured I/O bottleneck
- Teams already familiar with Tomcat tooling and ops practices
- Maximum compatibility with servlet-spec libraries

**When Jetty helps:**
- Workloads with many idle long-lived connections (WebSocket chat, SSE streams)
- Memory-constrained environments where idle footprint matters
- Existing Eclipse / OSGi ecosystems

**When Undertow helps:**
- Maximum servlet throughput on benchmarks
- HTTP/2 with the underlying XNIO non-blocking I/O
- Red Hat ecosystems (WildFly, JBoss EAP heritage)

**When Netty helps:**
- Spring WebFlux reactive applications — the default for a reason
- Thousands of concurrent connections on a small thread pool
- Streaming and back-pressure semantics

**Watch for:**
- Mixing blocking calls inside a Netty event loop — blocks the loop, kills throughput
- Switching to a server before measuring the actual bottleneck
- Server-specific properties (`server.tomcat.*`) silently ignored after a server swap
- Terminating TLS at the application when the platform (ingress, service mesh) could do it more efficiently

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Switch servers by excluding `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` and adding the alternative** — no code changes; Spring Boot auto-detects the server on the classpath.
- **WebFlux uses Netty by default, not Tomcat** — Netty is non-blocking and event-loop-based; Tomcat is blocking and thread-per-request; choosing between them drives the entire concurrency model.
- **`server.tomcat.threads.max` defaults to 200** — each thread handles one request; the ceiling on concurrent requests at blocking Tomcat is the thread pool size; too low causes request queuing under load.
- **SSL configuration: `server.ssl.key-store-type=PKCS12`** — use a keystore to terminate TLS at the application; in Kubernetes, prefer terminating TLS at the ingress controller or service mesh instead.
- **`server.compression.enabled=true` with `minimum-response-size`** — compresses responses above the threshold; reduces payload size for JSON-heavy APIs with no application code changes.
- **`WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T>` for server-specific tuning** — guard with `@ConditionalOnClass` so the bean only activates for the matching server.
- **`server.shutdown=graceful`** — combined with `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`, allows in-flight requests to complete before the JVM exits.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot embeds the web server inside the JAR — Tomcat by default, with Jetty, Undertow, and Netty as alternatives. Choosing and configuring the right server affects throughput, memory usage, and the concurrency model.

**Switching servers**
- Exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`
- Spring Boot auto-detects the server implementation on the classpath — no code changes required
- WebFlux applications use Netty by default; Netty is non-blocking and handles thousands of concurrent connections on a small thread pool; Tomcat uses one thread per request

**Key Tomcat settings**
- `server.tomcat.threads.max=200` (default) — the maximum number of simultaneous requests; increase for high-concurrency workloads, but each thread consumes memory
- `server.tomcat.accept-count` — the queue depth when all threads are busy; requests beyond this are rejected

**Common configuration**
- `server.port=8080`, `server.compression.enabled=true`, `server.ssl.key-store` — configured via `application.properties` without touching code
- `server.shutdown=graceful` — allows in-flight requests to complete before the JVM exits

**Programmatic customization**
- `WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory>` exposes server-specific knobs that have no property equivalent
- Guard with `@ConditionalOnClass` so the bean activates only when the matching server is on the classpath

The decision between Tomcat and Netty is architectural: blocking I/O with Tomcat suits traditional request-response Spring MVC; non-blocking event-loop Netty suits reactive WebFlux. Do not mix — using a blocking call inside a Netty event loop blocks the loop and kills throughput.

questions.question: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow — when should you actually switch from the default?
questions.title: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow — When to Switch
questions.direct_answer: **Don't switch without a measured reason**. Tomcat is the default because it handles most workloads well and has the broadest tooling and documentation. Switch to **Undertow** when measured `tomcat.threads.busy` saturation is the bottleneck and the workload is heavily I/O-bound. Switch to **Jetty** when you need many idle long-lived connections (WebSocket chat, SSE) or memory footprint at low traffic matters. Switch to **Netty + WebFlux** when the architecture is genuinely reactive and you can avoid blocking calls. **Never benchmark the server in isolation** — the application logic, downstream latencies, and JVM tuning dominate any server-level differences in real workloads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can resist premature optimization and articulate measurable signals that justify a server change
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Switching to Undertow or Netty based on a synthetic 'hello world' benchmark without measuring the actual production bottleneck
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the diagnostic path: `/actuator/metrics` for thread saturation, GC logs for memory pressure, distributed traces for latency attribution; switching servers is the last step, not the first

sections.title: The Server Is Rarely the Bottleneck
sections.content:
**The default is the right choice for almost every Spring Boot app**.
- Tomcat handles tens of thousands of requests per second per JVM in realistic workloads.
- Most production performance issues are downstream — database query plans, N+1 queries, slow external APIs, contended locks, GC pressure — and switching the embedded server changes none of that.

The **measurable signals** that justify a switch are specific.
- Thread pool saturation that holds steady at 90%+ even after async-ing slow operations suggests a non-blocking server might help.
- Memory pressure on idle pods at low traffic suggests a lighter footprint server.
- Tens of thousands of concurrent long-lived connections (WebSocket, SSE) suggest a non-blocking model.
- **None of these are diagnosed by a synthetic benchmark** — they show up in production metrics, traces, and GC logs.

The interview pitfall is the candidate who reaches for Undertow or Netty as a default optimization without evidence. The interviewer-impressing answer is the opposite: **Tomcat first, measure second, switch last**. And when you do switch, change one variable at a time so the impact is attributable.

sections.title: Decision Matrix — Symptom to Server Choice
sections.content:
Each row maps a measured production symptom to the candidate solution and what evidence justifies it.

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Server Choice | Evidence Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tomcat.threads.busy` consistently 90%+ | Slow downstream calls blocking request threads | Move slow calls to `@Async` first; only then consider Undertow | Latency breakdown: app vs DB vs external API |
| Memory grows linearly with idle connections | Servlet thread-per-connection with WebSocket | Jetty (lower idle footprint) or Netty | Heap dump showing connection-related allocations |
| 10K+ concurrent persistent connections (chat, SSE) | Thread-per-request can't scale to that connection count | Netty + WebFlux (event loop) | Concurrent connection count from `tomcat.connections.current` |
| High p99 latency under load with low CPU | Thread pool queueing | Tune `threads.max` and `accept-count` first; then Undertow | `tomcat.threads.busy` and request queue depth |
| Slow startup time | Auto-config heavy or fat classpath | Server choice irrelevant — profile startup | Actuator startup tracking endpoint |
| Container OOM kills at idle | Excessive baseline heap usage | Jetty or Undertow may help | RSS vs heap from container metrics |

**The pattern**: every row demands measurement before the change. Switching servers without these signals is cargo cult engineering.

sections.title: Diagnostic Path Before Switching
sections.content:
**Step 1 — Confirm thread saturation, not application slowness**
- Add Actuator and `micrometer-registry-prometheus`
- Watch `tomcat.threads.busy` and `tomcat.threads.config.max` ratio
- If consistently 80%+, the thread pool is the bottleneck
- If thread usage is low but latency is high, the problem is elsewhere — DB, external calls, GC

**Step 2 — Trace request latency end-to-end**
- Enable Micrometer Tracing or Spring Cloud Sleuth
- Look at the breakdown: time in controller, time in DB, time in external HTTP
- A slow downstream service is not fixed by a faster web server

**Step 3 — Tune Tomcat first**

```properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=400
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare=20
server.tomcat.accept-count=200
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=20000
server.tomcat.max-keep-alive-requests=200
```

- Doubling threads is cheaper than switching servers and reverts cleanly if it doesn't help

**Step 4 — Move blocking work off request threads**

```java
@Async
public CompletableFuture<EnrichedOrder> enrich(Order order) {
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(externalApi.enrich(order));
}
```

- Frees Tomcat threads quickly; defers heavy lifting to a separate `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`
- Often eliminates the saturation that motivated the switch in the first place

**Step 5 — Only then consider switching**
- If steps 1-4 don't relieve the pressure, run a controlled A/B with Undertow
- Same instance size, same workload generator, same observability — measure before declaring victory

sections.title: When the Server Switch Is Genuinely the Right Call
sections.content:
**WebSocket-heavy applications**
- Chat apps, collaborative editing, live dashboards with 10K+ concurrent connections
- Tomcat thread-per-connection model becomes a memory ceiling
- Jetty handles many idle connections more efficiently; Netty + WebFlux scales further

**Streaming server-sent events**
- Long-lived HTTP connections that hold a thread in Tomcat indefinitely
- Undertow or Netty's non-blocking model frees the I/O thread between events

**Reactive architectures**
- Genuinely reactive code: WebFlux + R2DBC + reactive Kafka consumers
- Netty is the only server that matches the reactive model end-to-end
- Mixing blocking JDBC inside WebFlux + Netty defeats the entire purpose

**Memory-constrained sidecars**
- Service mesh sidecars or admin agents where heap budget is 64-128 MB
- Jetty has the lowest idle footprint; sidecar workloads rarely need throughput tuning

**A pragmatic rule**
- If you can't articulate the measured production signal, don't switch
- If the platform (Kubernetes ingress, API gateway) handles connection-level concerns, Tomcat is fine for the app

sections.title: Switch-or-Stay Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When switching helps:**
- Measured saturation that survives async-ification and thread-pool tuning
- Architectural shift to reactive that needs Netty's event loop
- Specialized workloads (WebSocket, SSE) at scale where idle connections dominate

**When switching hurts:**
- Premature optimization driven by synthetic benchmarks
- Loss of Tomcat-specific tooling, debug experience, and team knowledge
- Server-specific properties (`server.tomcat.*`) silently no-op after a switch
- Less ecosystem documentation for Undertow / Netty edge cases

**Watch for:**
- Mixing blocking calls into a reactive Netty stack — defeats the model and produces worse latency than Tomcat
- Forgetting to update server-specific tuning after the switch — defaults may not match prior behavior
- Different graceful-shutdown behavior — verify in-flight requests complete before pod termination
- Different default error pages and exception handling around protocol-level failures

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default to Tomcat** — broadest documentation, largest community, fine for most workloads.
- **Measure before switching** — `tomcat.threads.busy`, request latency breakdown, GC logs, RSS vs heap; without evidence, don't change.
- **Async first, then server change** — moving blocking work to `@Async` often eliminates the saturation that motivated the switch.
- **Undertow for max servlet throughput** — non-blocking XNIO I/O; switch only when measured thread saturation persists after tuning.
- **Jetty for many idle connections or low memory** — better idle footprint; classic choice for WebSocket and SSE workloads on the servlet stack.
- **Netty + WebFlux for genuinely reactive** — event loop matches reactive code; mixing blocking JDBC inside WebFlux defeats the purpose.
- **Server-specific properties are silently ignored after a switch** — `server.tomcat.*` does nothing under Jetty; re-audit configuration after migration.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The honest answer is: **don't switch without a measured reason**. Tomcat is the default for a reason — it handles most workloads well, has the broadest tooling, and is what most teams already debug confidently.

**The diagnostic path before any switch**
- Confirm saturation, not application slowness — look at `tomcat.threads.busy` vs `threads.config.max`
- Trace request latency end-to-end — slow downstream calls don't get faster with a different web server
- Tune Tomcat first — increase `threads.max`, raise `accept-count`, adjust `connection-timeout`
- Move blocking work to `@Async` — often eliminates the apparent need to switch

**When the switch is genuinely justified**
- Undertow when servlet throughput is the bottleneck and tuning didn't help
- Jetty when you have many idle long-lived connections (WebSocket, SSE) or need lower idle memory
- Netty + WebFlux when the architecture is genuinely reactive — and you can avoid blocking JDBC, blocking JMS, blocking HTTP clients

**The mistakes to avoid**
- Switching based on a synthetic benchmark — production behavior is dominated by application logic and downstream services
- Mixing blocking calls into a Netty reactive stack — worse than Tomcat, not better
- Forgetting that `server.tomcat.*` properties silently no-op after a switch — re-audit configuration

In an interview, the strongest answer is: **I'd default to Tomcat, instrument with Actuator and tracing, and only consider a server change after the diagnostic path points clearly to the I/O model as the bottleneck**. The server is rarely the bottleneck.
